![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/380b44a8baf8ed15eb3eb4e66e77b820f5bc51a73be840526db67d96f6d763ed.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.$*
worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le x\le \frac{1}{2}y}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/185f85445f95382afdd9516351f0cce3c4d2b11d99f65da2d5a36db0fc853215.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/6aeba17b071bd275be7147ffb925b488881a2fb8de5f544dbffe8caab5c036e4.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}y\,⟹\,y=2x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=2.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,2x\le y\le 2},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/be089ef60080ad9181db8a5dacccf6abe382bef492369342fa15761134b507d2.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by $x=\frac{1}{2}(2)=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/885b884fee574cae3c2f62ac0092e64b9be1731ae8510f6e910d0a101ffa3f20.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y/2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,dy\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[{\int }_{2x}^{2}\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2-2x}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2(1-x)}{(1+{x}^{2})(1-x)}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[z]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
